preamble: Definitions f or al l the solutions are normal, but some of them require a positive/negative switch (or vice versa) before entry in the grid, as indicated in their clue’s wordplay.

clue.text: Caged, eating endless insects, a bird

indicators.note: one thing eating another takes it inside, so the caged word goes round the rest

parts.note: pent, as in pent up, means shut in or caged

indicators.note: endless means the word for the insects loses its final letter

parts.note: lice are small parasitic insects

explanation.surface: A bird kept in a cage is fed on insects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims LICE to LIC; with A, 'eating' puts it inside PENT, giving PELICANT. Per the preamble, that is the bird PELICAN with CAN switched to negative CAN'T, and PELICANT is what goes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelican is a large water bird with a throat pouch for scooping fish.

clue.text: Forceful grabbing a round

definitions.note: an adjective here, meaning plump or rotund

indicators.note: the forceful word takes hold of the a, which ends up inside it

parts.note: punchy writing or play is vigorous and forceful
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aggressive boxer seizes the chance to land a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' reads like a boxing round, but it is an adjective for a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Paunchy describes someone with a pot belly, so rounded in shape.

clue.text: Very popular musician has five listeners gathered round piano? See about that!

indicators.note: the letters are gathered up and turned around into a new order
a second signal that the whole collection is rearranged

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
taken as written: all its letters go into the mix
p is the musical marking for soft playing
Ely in Cambridgeshire is a bishop's see, a cathedral seat

explanation.surface: A superstar plays to a tiny audience round a piano, and someone vows to challenge it.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters rearrange to ELVISNT PRESLEY: the preamble's switch turns the IS inside ELVIS into ISN'T, a dig at the 'Elvis lives' rumour, and that form goes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll, was among the best-selling solo artists in history.

clue.text: Grass to throw, only two thirds

indicators.note: keep just the first six of the nine letters, dropping the final three

parts.note: to bamboozle someone is to throw or confuse them

explanation.surface: Someone tosses grass but manages only part of the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw' means baffle here, not hurl.
explanation.definitionFit: Bamboo is a giant woody member of the grass family.

clue.text: Artist frames outstanding old chap with shaved head

indicators.note: standing out, i.e. on the outside, so the frames enclose the rest

parts.note: yokes are wooden frames fitted over the necks of oxen

indicators.note: the chap loses his first letter, his head

parts.note: boy is an informal word for a man, as in 'one of the boys'

explanation.surface: A painter puts a portrait of a remarkable bald old man in a frame.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds YOKOOYES: the switch turns the NO at the end of ONO into YES, so that form goes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoko Ono is a Japanese conceptual and performance artist, also known as John Lennon's widow.

clue.text: Something to drink, not drinking out of cap

indicators.note: the teetotal letters are taken out of the capping word

parts.note: to cap something is to better or outdo it
TT, teetotal, describes someone who never drinks alcohol

explanation.surface: A drink that someone sober refuses to take from a cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' looks like a hat, but it is the verb meaning outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer is the commonest alcoholic drink of all, brewed from malted grain and hops.

clue.text: Pedestrian pursuit of Members of Parliament under Blair's leadership

indicators.note: in a down answer the second part sits underneath the first
the leading letter of the name is taken

parts.note: Blair's first letter
a group of owls is called a parliament, so its members are owls

explanation.surface: A dull hobby for MPs during the Blair years.
explanation.walkthrough: The MPs are not politicians: a parliament is the collective noun for owls.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowls is a slow, gentle game played on a green, a sedate and unexciting pastime.

clue.text: Fighter's back to the middle, hurt

indicators.note: that letter is then put back in the centre of what remains
the fighter's last letter is lifted off the end

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight boxer
the last letter of Ali, the piece lifted off its back
that same last letter of Ali, now set back in the middle

explanation.surface: A boxer is sent back to the centre of the ring, injured.
explanation.definitionFit: To ail is to be ill or in pain, so the verb sits close to hurt.

clue.text: Laid-back character first to oppose man of strict judgments

indicators.note: laid back is read as set backwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a card is an eccentric, an amusing character

indicators.note: only the opening letter of oppose is used

parts.note: its first letter only

explanation.surface: A relaxed person is the first to stand against a harsh judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid-back' looks like the word for relaxed, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco was the Athenian lawgiver whose punishments were so harsh they gave us the word draconian.

clue.text: Instrument's uplifting tune's beginning, no awful note produced

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting up means the parts are read from bottom to top
only the first letter of tune is taken

parts.note: the first letter of tune
taken as written
dire means dreadful
G is one of the musical notes A to G
did means made or produced

explanation.surface: An instrument opens with an uplifting tune and avoids any dreadful note.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives DIDGERIDONT: the switch treats the final DO of DIDGERIDOO as a positive and makes it DON'T for the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The didgeridoo is the long wooden drone pipe of Aboriginal Australia, played with circular breathing.

clue.text: You twice said killer is a poet

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the letter that sounds like you, written twice, is pronounced as the name of another letter

parts.note: the letter U, which sounds like you, written twice
a hitman is a paid assassin

explanation.surface: Someone tells you twice over that a murderer writes verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Walt Whitman was the American poet of Leaves of Grass.

clue.text: Shakespearean character with flash clothing, one in employment as empress

indicators.note: the moment word wraps round the spirit

parts.note: a mo, short for moment, is an instant, a flash
Ariel is the airy spirit in The Tempest

indicators.note: the one goes inside the employment word

parts.note: use, as in putting something to use
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean player in a showy costume is cast as an empress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' reads as showy clothing, but it is the instant MO.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Louise of Austria became Empress of the French on marrying Napoleon in 1810.

clue.text: Suspect couple bound to be uncertain, legally

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means doubtful, so the letters are not to be trusted in this order

parts.note: II is the Roman numeral two, a couple
taken as written: its letters join the mix

explanation.surface: A couple under suspicion are fated to remain unsure where they stand in law.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the legal Latin tag, as in 'in dubio pro reo': when in doubt, find for the accused.
explanation.definitionFit: In dubio is Latin for 'in doubt', used by lawyers for a point not settled.

clue.text: Wet creature finds nucleus of fluid in dry feature

indicators.note: that centre letter is put inside the dry feature

parts.note: to sear is to scorch or dry up
the chin is a facial feature

indicators.note: the central letter of fluid

parts.note: the middle letter of this five-letter word

explanation.surface: A sea animal discovers moisture inside an arid landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet creature' sounds like a feeble person, but here it is simply an animal living in water.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea urchin is a spiny marine animal, so it lives in the wet.

clue.text: Lean on back of spade in wood

indicators.note: in an across answer, one part placed on another comes after it
the back of a word is its final letter, so the end of spade is taken

parts.note: its last letter
bony means thin, with no fat

explanation.surface: A gardener leans on the back of a spade among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean on' reads as a phrasal verb, but it splits: lean is BONY and on joins it to the spade's end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebony is the dense black hardwood used for piano keys and carving.

clue.text: Pig for the compost heap?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a contemptible, nasty person
second meaning, playfully: something that rots, as waste on a compost heap does

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented sense: one that rots.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotter is a cad or scoundrel, and the word also reads literally as anything that rots.

clue.text: US illustrator, reliable type with some skill

parts.note: a rock is a person you can always depend on
doing something well shows some skill

explanation.surface: An American artist is a dependable sort with a little talent.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Rockwell painted the much-loved Saturday Evening Post covers of small-town America.

clue.text: Monsters provided twisted tails

indicators.note: the little word is turned around

parts.note: if, as in 'provided that'
ends, the back parts of things

explanation.surface: Creatures supplied with curly tails turn out to be monsters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiends are demons or evil spirits, cruel monsters of legend.

clue.text: Some music died in a little light composition of the '60s

parts.note: a note is a single musical sound, a little piece of music

indicators.note: the letter for died goes inside the beam of light

parts.note: a ray is a thin beam, a small amount of light

explanation.surface: A short-lived tune fades out within a gentle piece written in the sixties.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds NOTERDAY, which is YESTERDAY with YES switched to NO, as the preamble asks; the grid takes the switched form.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesterday is the 1965 Beatles song written by Paul McCartney, a defining piece of that decade.

clue.text: Change around position in higher education

indicators.note: the change word goes round the position word

parts.note: to vary is to change
sit, as in a place to sit or a posture

explanation.surface: Someone switches jobs within a university.
explanation.walkthrough: VARSITY is the old British word for a university, now chiefly heard in sports matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Varsity is an informal word for a university, so a place of higher education.

clue.text: See 3
Seeds to eat when you are out of liqueur

indicators.note: those letters are taken out of the liqueur

parts.note: curacao is an orange-flavoured liqueur from the Caribbean
UR is text-speak for you are

explanation.surface: Some edible seeds appear once your bottle of liqueur runs dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacao beans are the seeds from which chocolate and cocoa are made.

clue.text: Religious work ending in conflict within Biblical land, cut short

indicators.note: that letter sits inside the shortened land
the land loses its last letter

parts.note: Canaan is the promised land of the Old Testament

indicators.note: the final letter of conflict

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: A sacred piece describes the end of a war in a truncated Holy Land.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives CANATA: the switch turns the CANT in CANTATA into the positive CAN, and that form goes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a choral work, often sacred, like those Bach wrote for church services.

clue.text: Planes must be so in war, or hit when failing scrutiny, ultimately

indicators.note: letters that fail are broken down and rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written: these letters are rearranged

indicators.note: the last letter of scrutiny

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: Wartime aircraft must pass inspection, or be struck down when they fail it.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft must be certified airworthy, fit and safe to fly, before it takes off.

clue.text: Shilling in money, nothing for poet

indicators.note: the shilling goes inside the money

parts.note: the yen is Japan's currency
S is the abbreviation for the old shilling, from the Latin solidus
O, the figure zero

explanation.surface: A poet is paid a shilling, then nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives YESNO: in NOYES the switch turns NO into YES and YES into NO, and the grid takes that form.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Noyes was the English poet of The Highwayman.

clue.text: See 26
More than one ridiculous work, it proves irksome

parts.note: SA, sex appeal, is crossword shorthand for it
something that tires you is wearisome

explanation.surface: A silly piece of writing finds that its humour soon grates.
explanation.definitionFit: A satire uses ridicule to expose folly, so satires are works that make things ridiculous.

clue.text: Second not the sixth drink

indicators.note: the sixth letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: the latter is the second of two things mentioned

explanation.surface: Someone orders a second round, but skips their sixth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a moment of time, but it means the latter of two.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is espresso with a large amount of steamed milk, a coffee drink.

clue.text: Cut in fashion, formal wear a fright

indicators.note: the cutting word goes inside the fashion word

parts.note: ton is an old word for high fashion, as in bon ton
to hew is to cut with an axe
ties, as worn with dinner suits

explanation.surface: A haircut in the latest style, worn with formal dress, looks a fright.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds THE WONTIES: the switch turns the WILL in WILLIES into WON'T, and that form goes in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The willies is an informal term for a feeling of nervous fear or the creeps.

clue.text: Last of gravy in red sauce

indicators.note: that letter goes inside the Communist leader

parts.note: Mao Zedong was the Chinese Communist leader, a Red

indicators.note: only the final letter of gravy

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: The final drop of gravy settles into a red sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks like the sauce's colour, but it is a Communist.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayo is the everyday short form of mayonnaise, the egg and oil sauce.
